tagline.text: A white-sand island in northern Iloilo loved even before Boracay

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May (dry season, when the sea is calmest)

children.text: An island at the northern tip of Iloilo that was famous as one of the Philippines' top beach resorts in the 1970s, with a long white-sand beach, Tumakin Island reachable on foot at low tide, and Mount Opao overlooking the whole island. It suits travelers who want to relax on an uncrowded sea.
Sicogon Island is about
1,160 hectares
, floating off the coast of Carles, Iloilo, at the northeastern tip of Panay Island. It sits about
10km
from the mainland coast and about
146km
north of Iloilo City. The island is divided into three villages — Alipata, Buaya, and San Fernando — home to around 4,000 residents who fish and farm, and its highest point is Mount Opao at about
above sea level.
Though quiet today, Sicogon was one of the Philippines' leading beach resorts in the
. With its own airstrip and resort, people from Manila flew in directly, and it earned the nickname "Boracay before Boracay" during this era. But after the
, as Boracay and other islands rose in popularity and the resort closed, visitors stopped coming, and in November
, Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) struck the island and caused heavy damage.
Sicogon began to make a name for itself again in
, when Ayala Land and Sicogon Development Corporation, which owns land on the island, launched a joint redevelopment worth about
. The old airstrip was repaired and Sicogon Airport reopened in
, and nature-blended resorts such as Balay Kogon, Huni Sicogon, and Hatch Sicogon went up one after another. As losses piled up, however, flights to the airport ended in late
, and the joint venture that ran the resorts (SITEC) permanently closed its tourism estate facilities, including Huni Sicogon and Balay Kogon, on
. Disputes over resident relocation and land continue too: in
June 2026

Ayala Land handed over about 63 hectares as residential and farming land for residents, but more than 700 households are demanding the return of about 80 hectares. The island itself can still be visited freely, and the residents' villages are the center of island life.

Sicogon's charm lies in being "an island where you don't have to do anything." There's plenty to do — a long white-sand beach lined with coconut palms, Tumakin Island connected by a sandbar that appears at low tide, the Mount Opao viewpoint reached by a short hike, and island hopping to the nearby Islas de Gigantes — yet the crowds stay thin. It suits quiet couple's trips, family vacations with kids, and a northern Iloilo island trip combined with Islas de Gigantes.

The beach fronting Buaya village on the island's east side is considered Sicogon's best spot for a swim. The water is shallow and calm, great for playing with kids, and Tumakin Island sits right offshore.

blocks.title: Walking to Tumakin Island at Low Tide

children.text: Tumakin Island, an uninhabited islet off Buaya, reveals a sandbar path at low tide that you can walk across. Check the tide table and cross with a local guide.
At about
above sea level, Mount Opao is a short hike reaching the summit in
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
. From the top, you can take in Tumakin Island and its sandbar, along with the sea and islands toward San Dionisio on the mainland.

blocks.title: A Walk on San Fernando Beach

children.text: The long beach fronting San Fernando village is great for a sunset stroll, kayaking, and paddleboarding. At low tide, a wide mudflat is exposed, turning the scene into something entirely different.
About
1 hour
away by boat, Islas de Gigantes offers an island-hopping route taking in the viewpoint on Cabugao Gamay Island, the sandbar on Antonia Island, and Tangke Lagoon, all doable in a single day.
Hire a bangka to circle the island, taking in limestone coastline, small beaches, and snorkeling spots. Prices start around
per boat and vary by route.
Carles is so rich in seafood it's called "the Alaska of the Philippines." Be sure to try the scallops, crab, and kilawin, fish cured in vinegar.

For 3 days, 2 nights, it's a relaxed pace to spend the whole second day on Islas de Gigantes hopping and take a morning boat back to the mainland on day three. Boat schedules shift with the tide and weather, so confirm with your accommodation the day before.
The nearest airport is Roxas Airport (RXS) in Capiz province, about
1 hour
from Manila, with Roxas to Estancia port about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by car.
Iloilo International Airport (ILO), which has more flight options, is about
1 hour 10 minutes
from Manila. From the airport to Estancia is about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
by car.
AirSWIFT ran flights from Manila to Sicogon Airport (ICO) on the island, but service stopped in late
, and AirSWIFT itself was merged into Cebgo in
July 2026
. There are no scheduled flights now, so use Roxas or Iloilo airport.
From the Tagbak Terminal (the northbound terminal) in Jaro district, Iloilo City, Ceres buses and vans to Estancia and Carles run from dawn. It takes about
3–4 hours
and costs about
one way.
From Roxas City, it's about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
to Estancia by van or bus. Coming from Boracay (Caticlan) or Kalibo, allow about
5–6 hours
via Roxas.
Passenger bangkas to Sicogon run mainly in the morning from Estancia port. It takes about
45 minutes–1 hour
, for around
per person. Boats leaving the island often depart early in the morning.
You can also take a boat from Bancal port in Carles, which takes about
30 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
. At the tourist information office at Bancal port, you register, book a boat, and pay the environmental fee.

If you stay at a homestay, ask the owner in advance to meet you at Estancia or Bancal port and arrange the boat connection. If you miss the shared boat, you'll have to call a chartered boat, and the cost rises sharply.
There are almost no cars on the island, so you walk or take a motorbike taxi, habal-habal (about
per person).
March–May
brings weak winds and calm seas, making it the most reliable time for boats and island hopping. Clear skies make the sand and sea colors at their most vivid, and midday temperatures climb to around
December–February
is also dry season, but the northeast monsoon (Amihan) roughens the sea east of the island, and the Estancia–Sicogon boat can get bumpy or be cancelled on some days.
June–November
is the rainy and typhoon season. Especially in
August–November
, when a typhoon passes over the Visayas, boats may not sail for days at a time, so leave a day of slack in your schedule. During Holy Week and the early
May

holidays, domestic travelers crowd in and lodging and boats fill up quickly, so book ahead. The crossing to Tumakin Island and the beach scenery change greatly with the tides, so it helps to check the tide table before you leave.

For a while, Sicogon's lodging centered on Ayala-affiliated resorts (Balay Kogon, Huni Sicogon, and others), but operator SITEC permanently closed the tourism estate facilities on
, so you can't stay at a resort now. What remains are simple homestays and beach cottages in the villages of Buaya and San Fernando, and judging by island homestay rates elsewhere in Carles, about

per night. Iloilo province and Carles municipality are preparing a "Turista sa Barangay" program to develop island residents' homes into Department of Tourism-accredited homestays, so ask the Carles tourism office for the latest homestay information. If you can't find a room on the island, you can also stay on the mainland in Estancia or Carles and visit as a day trip.

There are almost no restaurants on the island, so most meals are at the homestay. Scallops caught off Carles are eaten grilled with butter and garlic or steamed, and you can try Iloilo home cooking such as steamed crab, kilawin (raw fish cured in vinegar and ginger), binakol (chicken and vegetable soup), and KBL, an Ilonggo soup of beans, pork, and jackfruit. If you're staying at a homestay, it's best to order the meals ahead the day before.
The island has no ATM, or a very limited one. Withdraw plenty of cash in Iloilo or Roxas beforehand.
Cell signal and Wi-Fi are inconsistent depending on location and carrier. Handle anything urgent while still on the mainland.
Tumakin Island can only be crossed on foot at low tide. Check the tide schedule and move with a guide so you return before the water comes back in.
Climb Mount Opao with a local guide and bring lace-up shoes and water. Early morning or late afternoon is cooler than midday.
To combine this with Islas de Gigantes, either charter a hopping boat from Sicogon, or take a joiner tour from Bancal port that links both destinations for an easy trip.
There are almost no pharmacies or convenience stores on the island. Bring basic medicine, sunscreen, and insect repellent from the mainland.
Ask permission before photographing villagers, and keep boats away from fishing grounds and aquaculture pens.
The small bangkas running between Estancia/Bancal and Sicogon rock easily in waves. Always wear a life vest, and don't push it on days when the coast guard halts departures.
Boats can be cancelled suddenly during
December–February
, when the northeast monsoon is strong, and during typhoon season. It's safer to be back on the mainland the day before your flight home.
The mudflats and rocks exposed at low tide harbor sea urchins and sharp shells. Wear aqua shoes.
There's no major hospital on the island; the nearest ones are on the mainland toward Estancia and Carles. Avoid overexerting yourself in the water or swimming after drinking.
There's a boundary between the resort area and resident villages. Don't enter areas marked private property, and respect residents' living spaces.
The Huni Sicogon and Balay Kogon facilities that closed in
June 2026
are guarded by security, with no-entry signs posted. Because of the land dispute, on
June 25–26
armed people entered the resorts and faced off with police, so don't go near facilities in dispute and follow the guidance of the Carles tourism office and police.
Environmental fees, boat fares and schedules, and whether flights are operating all change often, so check the latest notices before you go.
